titulo.texto: The Fusion of Two Cultures: González Camarena’s Mural

frase_gancho.texto: A Spanish soldier and a figure with an eagle’s head, both wounded: this is how González Camarena imagined the origin of Mexico.

puente_narrativo.texto: Before leaving this room, look for Jorge González Camarena’s mural: a Spanish soldier and a figure with an eagle’s head face each other in an image of the origin of Mexico.

guion_corto.texto: Where does Mexican culture come from? In nineteen sixty-three, Jorge González Camarena answered with an image of combat. On one side, a Spanish soldier on horseback. On the other, a figure with an animal body and an eagle’s head, symbolizing the peoples of Mesoamerica. Both are in a fighting stance, and both are wounded by the hand of their enemy. There is no clear victor. The painter meant that something new was born from that violent clash. It is an idea much repeated in the twentieth century, and it deserves a critical eye. Notice the postures and the wounds, and keep this image in mind to compare it later with another mural by the same artist.

guion_largo.texto:
A horse, a soldier and, facing them, a creature with an eagle’s head. This is The Fusion of Two Cultures, the mural Jorge González Camarena painted in nineteen sixty-three. It is one of the most discussed images in the first rooms of the museum, and it is not a gentle scene.

The composition is a duel. On one side is the Spaniard, on his horse. On the other, a body in the form of an animal with an eagle’s head, which symbolizes the races of Mesoamerica. Both are in a fighting stance. And both are wounded by the hand of their enemy. The painter avoids giving a winner and puts both sides on an equal footing of pain.

The title explains the message. According to the mural, Mexican culture was born of the clash between Nahuatl and Spanish civilizations, through war and violence. The word fusion sounds soft, but the image is not. What joins the two figures is a shared wound.

The real history was more complex than a duel between two characters. In fifteen twenty-one, the fall of Tenochtitlan was the result of war, of diseases such as smallpox and of alliances with Indigenous peoples who were fighting against the Mexica. It is what you saw in the previous room, with the [Tzompantli of Tecoaque](chap_04_encuentro_conquista): there, violence appears without rosy or dark legends. This mural carries it into the language of symbol.

González Camarena is known for another famous image: La Patria, the woman with the national coat of arms who illustrated the cover of the free textbooks. With that cover and with this mural, he helped give visual form to an idea of the nation in the twentieth century.

It should be said with care that this idea, of a nation born of mixture, has been much debated. For some historians and for many Indigenous peoples, it erases those who kept on existing with their languages and cultures. Mexico today has dozens of living Indigenous peoples. That is why the mural is better understood as an interpretation of its time than as a neutral description of the past.

That takes nothing away from its value. On the contrary: a mural like this lets us see how history was told in the nineteen sixties and what the visitor was meant to feel. The museum keeps these works precisely so that we read them, and also so that we discuss them.

Notice the posture of the two figures and the wounds the painter chose to show. Ask yourself why he chose a soldier on horseback and a figure with an eagle’s head, and not ordinary people. The symbols make the scene seem to belong to all times, and that is part of its strength.

Keep this image. The same painter signed the mural of [the Constitution of nineteen seventeen](chap_11_constitucion_1917), almost at the end of the tour of the museum. One opens the story of modern Mexico and the other closes it. If you compare them, you will notice the change in tone: here, the pain of the clash; there, the writing of a law.

texto: Look for the Spanish soldier on horseback
Find the figure with an animal body and an eagle’s head
Notice the wounds of both figures and their fighting stance

texto.Theme: The origin of Mexican culture in the clash between the Nahuatl and Spanish worlds
texto.Figures: A Spanish soldier on horseback and a figure with an animal body and an eagle’s head

texto.pregunta: Myth: The mural shows the victory of the Spaniards over the Mexica.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It shows both figures wounded and in a fighting stance, with no victor. It is an allegory about the birth of Mexican culture, not an account of a specific battle.
